starshipEstimatedLaunch.summary: SpaceX’s launch page does not list an official Flight 14 date. As of September 5, Next Spaceflight continues to list the first orbital Starship attempt as no earlier than September 15, 2026; no precise launch time is defensible.

stories.title: NASA's Starling satellites demonstrate GPS-free autonomous navigation
stories.summary: The FALCON experiment used onboard cameras and a catalog of space objects to determine Starling's orbit without GPS or ground navigation. Over three days it also improved orbit estimates for more than 200 tracked objects, a step toward autonomous lunar satellite swarms and better collision avoidance.

stories.title: NASA's Roman telescope clears its flight-readiness review
stories.summary: NASA and SpaceX certified the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope to proceed into final launch preparations, targeting no earlier than 7:26 a.m. EDT on August 30 aboard Falcon Heavy. Roman's wide-field surveys are designed to study dark energy, dark matter, exoplanets, and the universe's evolution.

stories.title: Hubble identifies a major merger from the Milky Way’s infancy
stories.summary: Hubble measurements of 39 inner-Milky-Way globular clusters, combined with Gaia data, isolate a third cluster population that points to an ancient collision with a dwarf galaxy dubbed LKH. The result pushes definitive evidence of the Galaxy’s assembly history about 1.8 billion years farther back, to roughly 11.8 billion years ago.

stories.title: NASA begins its most flight-relevant lunar landing plume tests
stories.summary: NASA has begun firing a simulated lander plume into lunar-regolith simulant inside a 60-foot vacuum sphere at Langley. Cameras and other instruments are measuring crater formation, ejecta geometry, and particle speeds to validate models for how rocket exhaust could endanger landers, surface equipment, and crews on the Moon—and eventually help prepare for Mars landings.

stories.title: NASA’s newest deep-space antenna begins operations at Goldstone
stories.summary: NASA’s 34-meter Deep Space Station 23 antenna has entered service after completing its test campaign, already tracking Chandra and communicating with missions including Psyche, Juno, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and Voyager 1. The new multifrequency dish expands the Deep Space Network’s capacity for the growing fleet of deep-space missions and is a completed, operational infrastructure milestone.

stories.title: Europe launches a high-frequency weather imager for severe-storm nowcasting
stories.summary: ESA launched the MTG-I2 weather satellite aboard Ariane 6, completing the first operational trio of Meteosat Third Generation satellites. Once commissioned, its Flexible Combined Imager and Lightning Imager will provide high-resolution views of developing weather across Europe and northern Africa every 2.5 minutes, strengthening severe-weather, wildfire, pollution, and climate monitoring.

stories.title: NASA’s Swift observatory resumes X-ray and ultraviolet science
stories.summary: NASA has restarted Swift’s X-ray and ultraviolet/optical instruments after months in low-drag mode intended to preserve the observatory for an attempted orbital boost. The boost spacecraft will no longer capture Swift, but the 21-year-old mission can again rapidly observe transient cosmic events while NASA estimates it has roughly one to two months above the altitude where operations become difficult.
stories.caveat: Swift’s third instrument, the Burst Alert Telescope, remains offline as the team works to return it to data collection.

stories.title: NASA’s Roman telescope launches toward its dark-universe survey
stories.summary: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched aboard a Falcon Heavy and separated from the rocket’s second stage, beginning its roughly three-month journey to the Sun–Earth L2 point. After commissioning, Roman will conduct wide, deep visible-to-near-infrared surveys to probe dark energy and dark matter and build a census of exoplanets.

stories.title: NOAA’s long-range robots extend a seafloor survey where ships cannot go
stories.summary: NOAA Fisheries sent two long-range autonomous underwater vehicles along more than 200 nautical miles of Mid-Atlantic seafloor track lines, collecting over 68,000 images for the Atlantic sea-scallop assessment. Their camera, environmental, and navigation systems can sample inside and around offshore infrastructure where traditional survey vessels cannot safely operate; NOAA says comparable robot data have already passed technical review and entered annual abundance estimates.

stories.title: Satellite record reveals a rapid post-2014 intensification of the Gulf Stream
stories.summary: A NOAA and University of Miami study of 31 years of satellite-altimeter observations found that the Gulf Stream downstream of the Florida Straits weakened until 2014, then shifted northward, stabilized, and rapidly strengthened through 2023. The result ties the change to wind-driven strengthening of the subtropical gyre and matters for North Atlantic heat transport, weather, sea level, and marine ecosystems.

source.name: NOAA Atlantic Oceanographic and Meteorological Laboratory

stories.caveat: The observed downstream Gulf Stream change should not be read as a direct measure of the broader Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC), which responds to different forcings.

stories.title: ESA records a precision-targeted satellite reentry for debris science
stories.summary: ESA deliberately guided the Cluster satellite Samba to a remote South Pacific reentry and flew an instrumented aircraft from Tonga to observe it. The satellite reentered at 21:39:38 UTC on August 31, with the final prediction accurate to the second; 29 of 30 airborne instruments recorded its breakup, yielding rare measurements of how a spacecraft heats, fragments, and sheds materials.
stories.caveat: ESA says the images and instrument data are still being processed, so detailed material-by-material results are not yet available.

stories.title: Hubble finds a giant, evolving decagon around Saturn’s south pole
stories.summary: NASA’s Hubble observations have revealed a 10-sided atmospheric wave embedded in Saturn’s south-polar jet stream—the first large regular-sided jet pattern seen in the planet’s southern hemisphere. The structure reaches through multiple atmospheric layers and had faint precursors in data from 2023, giving researchers a chance to watch a giant-planet circulation pattern develop.
stories.caveat: Scientists do not yet know whether the new decagon will become a long-lived stable feature like Saturn’s northern hexagon or continue evolving.

stories.title: A multi-sensor rocket finds unexpected structure in radio-disrupting ionospheric clouds
stories.summary: New peer-reviewed results from NASA’s SpEED Demon sounding rocket provide the first simultaneous multi-point measurements inside a sporadic-E layer, a metal-ion cloud that can disrupt long-distance radio and GPS signals. Five detectors showed the layer was uneven and structured rather than a simple sheet, including a split into two peaks during descent—evidence that atmospheric turbulence shapes the plasma.
stories.caveat: The proposed Kelvin–Helmholtz turbulence explanation is plausible but unconfirmed because the flight did not directly measure local winds and electric fields.

stories.title: BepiColombo successfully sheds its transfer stage on approach to Mercury
stories.summary: After almost eight years and billions of kilometres in flight, ESA and JAXA’s BepiColombo mission successfully separated its Mercury Transfer Module more than 200 million kilometres from Earth. The Mercury Planetary Orbiter and Magnetospheric Orbiter are now operating as a composite spacecraft on the next leg toward Mercury orbit insertion in November, a key milestone toward the first two-spacecraft scientific mission at the planet.
stories.caveat: The two orbiters have not yet entered Mercury orbit; ESA schedules orbital insertion for November 2026 and science operations for April 2027.

stories.title: NASA’s X-59 completes 25 flights with flight behavior matching its models
stories.summary: NASA’s quiet-supersonic X-59 research aircraft has completed 25 test flights, including a 72-minute flight to Mach 1.2 and 49,000 feet. NASA reports that its handling, stability margin, and flight loads have closely matched the preflight digital-twin predictions, without unexpected aerodynamic instability or excessive vibration—clearing the way for acoustic-validation flights that will directly measure its low-boom sonic thumps.
stories.caveat: The key low-boom claim is not yet validated: NASA’s dedicated acoustic measurement campaign is the next phase.
